The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(2,1)$ and $B(2,4).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=-3\sqrt{y}\,i+3\sqrt{x}\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux in a Source-Free Vector Field
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/f9b1b286210d694cd3786fe38190216da503bfa3223114f86c8706f810313e33.png)

The curve $C_1$ has endpoints $A(5,3)$ and $B(1,3).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\sqrt{y^3}\,\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\,\mathbf{j}
$$

 through $C_1$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector  $\mathbf{n}_1,$ as shown above. 

*Hint: You're given that $\mathbf F$ is source-free.*
examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

First, notice that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,
$$

where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png)

Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5})-(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}.
$$

What is the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ across the curve $C$ shown above?

*Hint: Start by checking whether $F$ is source-free.*
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero.
Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$
